title: Cleaning instruments: manual, ultrasonic & washer-disinfector
blurb: Why cleaning comes before sterilising, the three cleaning methods compared, and how to inspect what comes out.
question: The practice washer-disinfector has broken down and the engineer can't come until tomorrow. The dentist asks you to clean today's instruments by hand. How do you clean them safely and effectively, and why is the washer-disinfector normally the preferred method?

teach.body: Steam can only kill what it touches. Blood, saliva, tissue and set dental materials shield microorganisms from the steam, and once baked on they are even harder to remove. Prion proteins are not reliably destroyed by steam at all, so physically washing protein off is essential. That is why HTM 01-05 calls effective cleaning an essential prerequisite for sterilisation. An instrument that is still visibly soiled never goes forward: it goes back to be cleaned again.

teach.caption: HTM 01-05 lists three routes: washer-disinfector; manual combined with ultrasonic; manual alone. Every practice still needs a trained manual-cleaning backup.

steps.label: Thermal disinfection
steps.sub: e.g. 80 °C for 10 min or 90 °C for 1 min

teach.caption: Because the cycle ends with a disinfection stage, instruments come out safe to handle and inspect.

teach.h: Why the first flush is cool
teach.body: Blood is full of protein, and protein coagulates when heated, just like an egg white turning solid in a hot pan. Coagulated protein sticks to steel and is very hard to shift. So the washer-disinfector's first flush uses water below 45 °C, and in manual cleaning you check with a mercury-free thermometer that the water stays at 45 °C or lower. Heat comes later, once the soil has gone.

items.label: flush and manual-wash water, so protein doesn't fix on
minimum time to keep washer-disinfector records

items: Wash hands and put on PPE: apron, mask, eye protection, then heavy-duty gloves.
Use two dedicated sinks or bowls, one to wash and one to rinse. Never the wash-hand basin.
Measure water and an instrument detergent to the right concentration, at 45 °C or lower.
Dismantle and open instruments, then fully immerse them.
Scrub under the water with a long-handled, soft plastic brush, so no aerosol is made.
Rinse in the second sink with potable, distilled or RO water, then drain (and dry if wrapping).
Inspect under an illuminated magnifier, then complete any records.

teach.body: Ultrasonic cleaners shake debris loose with high-frequency sound waves in the solution. Open hinges and dismantle instruments, then fully immerse them in the suspended basket. Never put them on the tank floor and never overload it. Close the lid and don't open it until the cycle ends, because the lid contains aerosols. Afterwards drain, rinse and inspect. Change the solution when it is heavily soiled, or at the end of every session, and drain the tank at the end of the day.

teach.caption: Use a non-oil-based lubricant only, so it doesn't stop steam reaching the metal.

teach.text: Washing-up liquid, soap and chlorhexidine hand scrub are NOT instrument detergents. HTM 01-05 warns that chlorhexidine actually makes proteins stick to steel. Wire brushes are also out: they scratch the protective surface layer and lead to corrosion.

items: Cleaning must come before sterilisation; visibly soiled instruments go back to be recleaned.
Washer-disinfector is preferred: validated, and it disinfects. Stages: flush, wash, rinse, thermal disinfection, dry.
Keep flush and manual-wash water below 45 °C so protein doesn't coagulate.
Open hinges and don't overload, in any machine.
Inspect everything under an illuminated magnifier before packing.

summary: You can now explain why cleaning must come before sterilisation, compare manual, ultrasonic and washer-disinfector cleaning, name the washer-disinfector stages and why the first flush is cool, carry out manual cleaning safely, and decide what happens to an instrument at inspection.

A.q: Why does the first flush of a washer-disinfector use water below 45 °C?
options: To save energy before the wash stage
To stop protein coagulating onto instruments
To protect the machine's door seal
To activate the enzymatic detergent before washing
A.why: Hotter water coagulates protein such as blood and fixes it onto the instrument, making it much harder to remove.

whyNot.0: Energy saving isn't the reason given in HTM 01-05.
whyNot.2: Door seals are not why the flush is kept cool.
whyNot.3: Detergent works in the wash stage; the cool flush is about not fixing protein.

A.q: While packing, you notice dried blood in the joint of a pair of tweezers that has been through the washer-disinfector. What should you do?
options: Pack it, as the sterilizer will kill any bacteria
Wipe the joint with an alcohol wipe and pack it
Discard it in the sharps bin straight away
Send it back to be cleaned again before packing
A.why: Visibly soiled instruments must be recleaned. Soil shields microorganisms from steam, so sterilisation can't make up for poor cleaning.

whyNot.0: Steam can't penetrate debris, so the instrument would not be reliably sterilised.
whyNot.1: A wipe won't reliably remove soil from a joint, and alcohol can fix protein.
whyNot.2: Soiled but undamaged instruments are recleaned, not discarded.

A.q: Which statement about manual cleaning is correct under HTM 01-05?
options: It is the preferred method in best practice
It is fully validated like a washer-disinfector
It carries the highest risk of sharps injury
It includes a thermal disinfection stage
A.why: Manual cleaning is the hardest method to validate and carries a greater risk of inoculation injury, so it is a backup rather than the preferred method.

whyNot.0: A washer-disinfector is the preferred method.
whyNot.1: Manual cleaning can't be fully validated because it isn't automatic.
whyNot.3: Only a washer-disinfector has a thermal disinfection stage.

B.q: Which is the correct order of stages in a washer-disinfector cycle?
options: Wash, flush, disinfect, rinse, dry
Flush, disinfect, wash, rinse, dry
Rinse, wash, flush, dry, disinfect
Flush, wash, rinse, disinfect, dry
B.why: A typical cycle is flush (below 45 °C), wash, rinse, thermal disinfection, then drying.

whyNot.0: The cool flush has to come first, before any washing.
whyNot.1: Disinfecting before washing would fix soil on and leave it there.
whyNot.2: Drying is always last, and the flush is always first.

B.q: You are loading hinged instruments such as extraction forceps into the washer-disinfector. How should they be loaded?
options: Closed, so they take up less space
Stacked tightly to fill the basket
Opened fully, without overlapping
Wrapped in a pouch for protection
B.why: Hinges and joints must be fully open and instruments not overlapped, so every surface is exposed to the wash and disinfection.

whyNot.0: Closed hinges hide surfaces from the water and detergent.
whyNot.1: Overloading and overlapping lead to poor cleaning.
whyNot.3: Wrapping happens after cleaning and inspection, never before washing.

B.q: Which product should be used for manual cleaning of dental instruments?
options: A detergent made for instrument cleaning
Chlorhexidine hand scrub, diluted in water
Ordinary washing-up liquid
Liquid hand soap from the dispenser
B.why: HTM 01-05 says always use detergents specifically formulated for manual cleaning of instruments.

whyNot.1: Chlorhexidine makes proteins stick to steel.
whyNot.2: Washing-up liquid isn't designed for instruments and is specifically excluded.
whyNot.3: Soap is specifically excluded for instrument cleaning.

C.q: An ultrasonic cleaner is running. Why must the lid stay closed until the cycle has finished?
options: To contain aerosols released during cleaning
To keep the solution heated close to boiling point
To stop the timer from resetting itself
To allow the instruments to sterilise
C.why: Ultrasonic cleaning releases contaminated aerosols; the lid contains them.

whyNot.1: The solution isn't meant to boil.
whyNot.2: The lid is about aerosols, not the timer.
whyNot.3: Ultrasonic cleaners clean; they don't sterilise.

C.q: During manual cleaning, why are instruments scrubbed while fully under the water?
options: It makes the detergent foam more
It cools the water to below 45 °C
It reduces splashing and aerosols
It removes the need for a rinse sink
C.why: Keeping instruments submerged while scrubbing minimises splashing and aerosols, protecting the person cleaning.

whyNot.1: Submerging instruments doesn't change the water temperature.
whyNot.3: Instruments still need rinsing in a separate sink afterwards.

C.q: During inspection, a probe is found to be bent and slightly pitted. What should happen to it?
options: Lubricate it and pack it as normal
Run it through the ultrasonic again
Sterilise it on a longer cycle to be safe
Take it out of use to repair or discard
C.why: Blunt, bent, damaged or corroded instruments are removed from use and repaired or replaced.

whyNot.0: Lubrication doesn't fix damage or corrosion.
whyNot.1: Recleaning won't straighten it or remove pitting.
whyNot.2: A longer cycle doesn't make a damaged instrument safe or functional.

reteach.title: Think of washing a roasting tin
reteach.question: Why do you soak a roasting tin in cool water before scrubbing it, rather than blasting it with boiling water straight away?

blocks.body: Blast a dirty roasting tin with very hot water and the residue bakes on harder. Soak it cool, scrub it, rinse it, and only then use heat. Instruments are the same: cool water and detergent take the soil off, rinsing removes the detergent, and only then does heat (thermal disinfection, then sterilisation) finish the job. A washer-disinfector does all of this automatically and the same way every time, which is why it is preferred.

blocks.text: The sterilizer is not a backup for poor cleaning. If you can see soil, steam can't reach underneath it.

explain.body: Soil shields microorganisms from steam, and prion protein is only reliably reduced by washing it off. Cleaning is the essential first step, and anything visibly soiled is recleaned.

test.q: Why must instruments be cleaned before they are sterilised?
options: Debris shields microbes from the steam
The sterilizer cannot get hot enough
Cleaning makes the pouches seal properly
Sterilisation only works on wet items
test.why: Soil and debris prevent steam reaching the instrument surface, so microorganisms underneath survive.

whyNot.1: Sterilizers reach the right temperature; the problem is steam contact.
whyNot.2: Pouch sealing isn't why cleaning comes first.
whyNot.3: Instruments are dried before wrapping; wetness isn't the reason.

explain.body: The preferred method: automated, validated and reproducible. Five stages: flush below 45 °C, wash, rinse, thermal disinfection (for example 80 °C for 10 minutes or 90 °C for 1 minute), dry.

test.q: What makes a washer-disinfector the preferred cleaning method?
options: It sterilises the instruments fully
It is validated and includes disinfection
It removes the need for inspection afterwards
It can be used for single-use items
test.why: It cleans reproducibly under validated conditions and adds a thermal disinfection stage, making instruments safe to handle.

whyNot.2: Instruments must still be inspected afterwards.

explain.body: A backup, and acceptable at the essential quality level. Two sinks, instrument detergent, water at 45 °C or lower, instruments scrubbed under water with a long-handled soft brush, rinse, inspect.

test.q: During manual cleaning, what is the maximum temperature the wash water should reach?
test.why: HTM 01-05 says keep the water at 45 °C or lower, because a higher temperature coagulates protein and stops it being removed.

whyNot.0: 35 °C is within the safe range, but the stated upper limit is 45 °C.
whyNot.3: 80 °C is a thermal disinfection temperature, far too hot for washing.

explain.body: Sound waves shake debris loose. Use the basket, never the tank floor; don't overload; open hinges; keep the lid shut until the cycle ends; change the solution when heavily soiled or at the end of each session.

rows.label: Instruments placed on the tank floor

test.q: When should the solution in an ultrasonic cleaner be changed?
options: Once a week on Fridays
Only when it starts to smell
When heavily soiled or each session
Each time a foil ablation test is done
test.why: HTM 01-05 says change it when heavily contaminated or otherwise at the end of every clinical session, because debris reduces cleaning effectiveness.

whyNot.1: Smell is not the trigger; contamination and session end are.
whyNot.3: The foil test is periodic testing, not a schedule for changing solution.
